19814-three-years-in-france-with-the-gun:
Three Years in France with the Guns gives episodes in the life of a British artillery officer. One scene finds a subaltern waking from deep slumber in a train carriage. He peers out and groans at the beastly hole of Bouvette. His surprise at the laughter around him follows. The book's voice is dry, tired, and amused. It is the Western Front remembered by a gunner.

Artillery war was noise, mud, and long waiting between shoots. Officers' memoirs from the batteries are rarer than infantry ones. Episodes, rather than a grand narrative, suit that disjointed war. Humor carries scenes that horror would flatten. Readers get the guns' war at human scale. Such memoirs grounded Britain's memory of France.
19927-the-continental-monthly-vol-2-no-2:
The Continental Monthly for August 1862 is volume 2, number 2 of a wartime magazine. It declares itself devoted to literature and national policy. One story scene stands by a little run, four hundred yards from a farmhouse. A turpentine distillery occupies the bank there. Rosin and turpentine works scatter around it. Fiction, poetry, and war argument shared such numbers.

New York published the Continental through the Civil War's middle years. It mixed Southern scenes with Union politics deliberately. Turpentine country meant the pine barrens of the Carolinas. Stories grounded national policy in local color. A single issue shows the magazine's whole method. It remains useful to students of wartime print.
20565-the-continental-monthly-vol-6-no-2:
The Continental Monthly for August 1864, volume 6, number 2, mixes literature with the politics of a nation at war. The magazine spoke for the Union cause. Its essays scold the loose language of wartime debate as much as they praise the cause.

One writer complains that words like fool and tyrant are thrown at men the people have delighted to honor. Such language disgusts older and more thoughtful readers. It has become, he says, a recognized fact of the time. The issue shows how the Civil War filled even literary monthlies with argument about the nation's words and deeds.
22062-the-mathematicall-praeface-to-elem:
John Dee, Elizabeth I's famous astrologer-philosopher, wrote the Mathematicall Praeface for the first English Euclid in 1570. Henry Billingsley had translated the Elements of Geometrie; Dee's preface introduces it. He calls the preface very fruitful, specifying the chief mathematical sciences, what they are, and what they are good for. He also promises to disclose certain new mathematical and mechanical secrets, much missed until these days.

Dee maps arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, optics, music, and dozens of lesser arts in one great tree. He defends mathematics against charges of conjuring. The Praeface is a landmark of English science writing, and it made Dee's name across Europe. Readers still meet it as the gateway to Tudor mathematics.
22150-the-theories-of-darwin-and-their-r:
Eduard von Hartmann, the German philosopher, examined Darwin's theories and their bearing on philosophy, religion, and morals. His book, translated for English readers, addresses a troubled audience. Hartmann writes for people who feel they must set themselves right on these questions. They touch mankind's highest interests, yet few lay readers have time to master the sciences involved.

Hartmann argues that evolution and purpose need not be enemies. He defends a philosophy in which nature's process has meaning beyond blind chance. Religious and ethical views, he notes, remained sharply opposed after Darwin. The book is a period piece from the first great age of Darwin debates, when every thinker had to reckon with the new biology.
22690-rembrandt-and-his-works-comprising:
John Burnet wrote Rembrandt and His Works, a short account of the Dutch master's life and art, illustrated with examples from his etchings. The catalog record gives no year. Burnet, himself a painter and engraver, wrote for readers who admired Rembrandt but lacked access to the prints and paintings scattered across Europe.

In the preface, Burnet notes the limits set on the book's size and plates, while doing his publisher justice for sparing no expense to credit the great artist. Preparing the work showed him how wide the interest ran in making Rembrandt better appreciated. The text mixes biography with close looks at single etchings. It stands as an early English attempt to bring Rembrandt to a broad public, and it still reads with a practitioner's respect.
amenities-of-literature-consisting-of-sk:
Amenities of Literature, by Isaac Disraeli, collects sketches and characters of English literature. Disraeli, who wrote as Isaac D'Israeli and was the father of the prime minister, published the book in 1841 at the age of seventy-five; this edition dates from 1871. He meant it as a companion to his earlier Curiosities of Literature and Miscellanies of Literature.

The book was planned as part of a much larger work, a history of vernacular literature, that he never completed. What stands instead is a set of literary portraits and essays, written for pleasure by a lifelong man of letters. Readers get the elder Disraeli's hobby in bound form: anecdotal, curious criticism that preserves how the nineteenth century enjoyed its own literary past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acciajuoli:
Acciajuoli is the name of three cardinals from an illustrious Florentine family. Angelo, born in 1349 and dead at Pisa in 1408, was noted for learning, experience, and integrity. Urban VI made him Florence's archbishop in 1383 and cardinal in 1385, he resisted every effort to draw him to the antipope Clement VII. He defended Urban's election by word and deed.

After Urban's death, half the conclave's votes went to Acciajuoli, but he steered the election toward Boniface IX to end the schism. Boniface named him Ostia's cardinal-bishop, dispatching him to Germany, Slavonia, and Bulgaria. Niccolo, born in 1630, died at Rome in 1719 as Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia. Filippo, nuncio in Portugal, was expelled by Pombal in 1760 for backing the Jesuits and died at Ancona in 1766.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acephali:
Acephali, headless ones, is the term for Eutychians who withdrew from Peter Mongus, Monophysite head of Alexandria, in 482. Peter Mongus and Acacius of Constantinople had framed a new creed against Nestorius and Eutyches expressly, while passing over the Council of Chalcedon and rejecting it in bad faith. Emperor Zeno approved this vague formula and imposed it in his Henoticon, or edict of union.

The condemnation of Eutyches angered rigid Monophysites, and the unclear stance toward Chalcedon seemed insufficient. Many, especially monks, left Peter Mongus, choosing no head over staying in communion with him. Later they sided with Severus, Monophysite head of Antioch. Deacon Liberatus instead traces the name to Ephesus, to those following neither Alexandria's Cyril nor Antioch's John.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-advocatus-dia:
Advocatus Diaboli, Advocate of the Devil or Devil's Advocate, is the popular title of a leading officer of the Sacred Congregation of Rites. Sixtus V set up that body in 1587 to handle beatification and canonization cases. Promoter of the Faith, Promotor Fidei, is his official title; his duty is preparing in writing all possible arguments against raising anyone to the honours of the altar.

The church's interest and honour demand that no one receive honours whose death is not juridically proved precious in God's sight. Prospero Lambertini, later Benedict XIV, served twenty years as Promoter of the Faith and wrote his great work on beatification and canonization from that experience. No important act in the process counts unless done in the Promoter's formal presence. Urban VIII in 1631 made his presence, at least by deputy, necessary for validity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfonso-muzza:
Alfonso Muzzarelli was an Italian Jesuit, born at Ferrara in 1749 and dead at Paris in 1813. He joined the Jesuits in 1768, then taught at Bologna and Imola. After the order's suppression in 1773 he took a Ferrara benefice, then directed Parma's College of Nobles. Pius VII called him to Rome as Penitentiary theologian.

Exiled with Pius VII in 1809, Muzzarelli left Rome for Paris, where he spent his remaining years at a Paris convent. He wrote numerous theological and ascetical works. His chief production, The Good Use of Logic in Matters of Religion, gathers philosophico-theological treatises. It appeared in six volumes at Foligno in 1787 to 1789, ten at Rome in 1807, and eleven at Florence in 1821. It treats abuses in the Church, the pope's temporal power, toleration, indulgences, confession, and moral liberty. He also refuted Rousseau's Emile and Social Contract, and his Month of Mary reached about a hundred editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloysius-gent:
Aloysius Gentili was born at Rome in 1801 and died at Dublin in 1848. A poet and musician, mechanically and electrically inclined, devoted to languages, he lived as a brilliant young man of the world. Ambitious nobly, he was society's pet, fortune's favourite. He sought Jesuit admission, but his health prevented acceptance. Remaining in Rome, he attended lectures at the Irish College to improve his English, ordained in 1830, then made his novitiate at Domodossola.

At the Irish College, the convert Ambrose Phillips de Lisle asked for a priest to preach in England. Gentili served two years as Prior Park president, but Baines's mixing of secular and regular professors ended with the fathers' withdrawal. The first public mission at Loughborough, by Gentili and Furlong, succeeded, with sixty-three converts instructed and received. From 1844 to 1848 missions and retreats across England filled his years. At Newcastle 250 adult Protestants were received; three Manchester missions produced 378 converts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloysius-tapa:
Aloysius Taparelli, christened Prospero of the D'Azeglio family, was a philosopher and sociological writer, born at Turin in 1793, dead at Rome in 1862, buried near St. Aloysius's altar in St. Ignatius's. His father Cesare was Sardinian ambassador to the Holy See; his brother Massimo, an Italian minister of state. Educated by the Calasanctians at Siena and Turin's Atheneo, he attended St-Cyr for some months but soldiering was not his destiny. He entered the Jesuits at Rome in 1814.

In youth he showed a bent for mechanics, painting, music. He later invented the violicembolo, praised by Liszt, renamed the symphonium at his suggestion. He was first rector of the Roman College after its restoration to the Jesuits. He taught philosophy sixteen years at Palermo, then joined Civiltà Cattolica. His chief work, A Theoretical Essay on Natural Right, began modern sociology in a way. It was translated into German.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monopoli: Monopoli, the Apulian port of whitewashed houses, has been a bishop's see since Norman times. This entry covers its diocese, its cathedral, and its history on the Adriatic. The faith in the city of the single city: Monopoli's cathedral guards the Adriatic shore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nephtali: Naphtali was the sixth son of Jacob, and his tribe settled the fertile hills of Galilee. This entry covers the biblical tribe, its territory, and its history. The tribe of the northern hills: Deborah's victory was won on its territory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-niccolo-anton: Niccolo Zingarelli composed operas and sacred music for the churches of Naples and Milan in the early 1800s. This entry covers his career, his works, and his teaching. The maestro of two cities: his sacred music filled the cathedrals of Naples and Milan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicola-giacom: This biographical entry profiles Nicola Giacomo Mittarelli, an Italian Camaldolese historian of the 1700s, tracing his monastic career, his annals, and his scholarship as the 1913 editors recorded it. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolo-machia: Machiavelli wrote The Prince, the cold manual of power that made his name a synonym for cunning. This entry examines his career, his works, and the Church's judgment. The Florentine who unmasked politics: his Discourses praised republics as well as princes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolo-maria-: This biographical entry profiles Nicolo Maria Antonelli, an Italian cardinal and scholar of the 1700s, tracing his career, his learning, and his service to the Church as the 1913 editors recorded it. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paolo-dal-poz: Toscanelli was the Florentine cosmographer whose map encouraged Columbus to sail west. This entry covers his career, his science, and his influence. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petrus-aureol: Petrus Aureoli was the Franciscan theologian whose subtle metaphysics earned him the title of Doctor Facundus. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-castel: Pietro Castelli was the botanist who founded Rome's first botanical garden. This entry covers his career, his garden, and his works. The father of the Roman garden: his healing simples served the busy papal pharmacies of Baroque Rome daily for decades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-france: Mazzuchelli, called Morazzone, was the Lombard painter of the Counter-Reformation's fervor. This entry sketches his career, his frescoes, and his place. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pozzuoli: Pozzuoli, the ancient Puteoli of St. Paul's landing, became a diocese. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The Church at the apostle's Italian shore: its vast amphitheater saw the Christian martyrs die for Christ in holy faith and hope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-de-nob: Robert de Nobili was the Jesuit who became a Brahmin sannyasi. This entry traces his method, his mission, and his vindication. The apostle of Madura's Brahmins: his Brahmin thread marked the convert in Madura's mission field of India in the 1600s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rorate-coeli: Rorate Coeli is the Advent Mass of the dawn. This entry explains its name, its rite, and its beauty. The Mass of the dew's descent: its many candles pierce the dark of December's dawn in church and chapel and home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rotuli: The Rotuli are the liturgical rolls of the Middle Ages. This entry explains their form, their contents, and their survival. The scrolls of the chant: their parchment rolls preserved the music of the Office in the 1100s' choirs of the monks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ruggiero-giov: Ruggiero Giovanelli was the Roman composer of the polyphonic choir. This entry notes his motets, his mastership, and his art. The singer of the Sistine Chapel: his sweet polyphony filled Rome's chapels in the 1590s' Rome of the popes in song.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sandro-bottic: Sandro Botticelli was the painter of the Florentine spring. This entry examines his Madonnas, his mythologies, and his fame. The dreamer of the Medici court: his fair Venus crowns the Uffizi in Florence's gallery of the Medici's house in the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-savona-and-no: Savona and Noli became the diocese of the Ligurian coast. This entry covers its bishops, its cathedral, and its history. The faith of the Riviera towns: its baroque cathedral crowns Savona in Liguria's coast in the Riviera of the west.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scalimoli: Scalimoli, the name of the Italian theologian, carries a scholarly history. This brief entry notes his works and his fame. A quiet name from the schools: his learned pages served the students in the schools of Italy in the 1600s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-soli: Soli, the Cyprian city of the northern coast, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the island: its ancient ruins crown the coast in Cyprus' north in the Karpas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ambrose-of: St. Ambrose of Camaldoli was the humanist general. This entry traces his Camaldoli, his Greek, and his fame. The Traversari of the Florentine circle: his deep Greek enriched Camaldoli in the 1430s' Tuscany in the hermitage of the Apennines in the woods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eusebius-o: St. Eusebius of Vercelli was the bishop of the Piedmontese see. This entry traces his exile, his monastic clergy, and his fame. The confessor of the Arian age: his ancient see crowned Vercelli in the 340s' Piedmont in the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stefano-anton: Stefano Antonio Morcelli was the Jesuit antiquarian. This entry traces his inscriptions, his Chiari, and his fame. The epigraphist of the Italian church: his inscribed stones crowned Chiari in the 1780s' Brescia in the plain of the Oglio in Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syncelli: The Syncelli were the officers of the patriarch. This entry traces their cell and their duties. The attendants of the Byzantine throne: their monastic cell crowned the patriarch in the 700s' palace in the city of the very old Bosphorus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-takkali: Takkali was the mission of the north. This brief entry traces its priests and its work. A station of the early apostolate: its faithful priests crowned the mission in the 1800s' North in the territory of the very old traders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-termoli: Termoli is the diocese of Molise. This entry traces its see, its bishops, and its churches. The bishopric of the Adriatic port: its ancient see crowned Termoli in the 1000s' Biferno in the river of the truly very old coast.
cornelli:
Cornelli, by Johanna Spyri, is a story for children from the author of Heidi, presented to English readers in this translation for the first time. The foreword tells the whole arc honestly. Cornelli is a merry, beloved child. An unjust suspicion robs her of all life and mirth. Her lonely heart finds Dino, a sick boy who has suffered like her. Mux, a mischievous little fellow, helps unfold the tangle.

Spyri's pattern is Heidi's pattern moved to a new valley. A child's spirit is crushed by adult misunderstanding. Nature, friendship, and patience restore it. The foreword calls the book a tale for children and for those who love children. Its faith is the author's own: that no young heart is spoiled beyond the reach of sunshine and being believed. English readers met Cornelli decades after Heidi. The Alps of the telling are different. The medicine is the same.

doe-osti-3030827-strategic-pathways-for-: For many tribal communities, getting around means long drives on few roads — and breakdowns hit hard. This report maps out transportation plans built around Indigenous priorities: resilience when storms or supply chains fail, and new options like shared rides and cleaner vehicles. The goal is mobility that fits community life, not just car counts.

doe-osti-3818341-security-by-design-econ: Bolting security on at the end is expensive — building it in from the start is cheaper. Alan Scott Evans makes the economic case for security-by-design across the whole design lifecycle. The analysis shows where early security spending pays for itself many times over.
gallipoli: Gallipoli, John Masefield's history of the campaign. The Dardanelles tale. This book preserves that history. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. Writers of history may cite it later.
govdocs-archive_org-TonyBlairCullenGordo: Tag Archives: Lord Cullen - material on the Cullen inquiry touching Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, from the archive's tag collection. Declassified government document, preserved for researchers, complete, from the archive. Subject: government records. A public-record holding.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIALangerWillia:
William L. Langer was Harvard's great diplomatic historian and, in wartime, the chief of research and analysis for the OSS, the CIA's forerunner. This Washington Post obituary by Richard Pearson marks his death and sums up the double career.

Langer wrote standard histories of European diplomacy and then ran the analysts who briefed a president, later chairing the CIA's Board of National Estimates. Pearson's obituary column in the Post kept a running record of Washington's passing generations. The obituary is kept as the paper's farewell to the historian and intelligence chief.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DavisThomasEli_: A handwritten note dated July 7, 1977 was sent to J. Gary Shaw of Cleburne, Texas. The note concerns Thomas Eli Davis and the assassination of President Kennedy. Its signature is illegible and the text survives only in fragments, so the writer cannot be identified and the full point of the message cannot be recovered from what remains.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIOfficeofProf: A study titled The Security Investigation examines the FBI's surveillance and harassment of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. The Bureau's campaign against King is the whole subject: watching, listening, and pressure applied to the civil rights leader. The surviving record gives the study's title and subject but names no author or date, so it stands as a titled account of that campaign.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FulbrightJWilli:
A magazine profile titled The Roots of the Arkansas Questioner studies Senator J. William Fulbright of Arkansas. The profile centers on his role in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee's Vietnam hearings. Fulbright, once a supporter of the war's architects, had become their most respectable questioner on Capitol Hill.

The hearings gave doubt about Vietnam a Senate stage and a courteous southern voice. A profile reaching for the roots of that stance asks where the questioner came from. The magazine and author are not identified in the record, but the piece preserves how Fulbright was presented to readers then.
govdocs-archive_org-tibetan-religion-tit:
Giuseppe Tucci, the great Italian Tibetologist, traced how Buddhism first spread through Tibet in his book Tibetan Religion. He follows the meeting between Indian Buddhism, arriving from the south, and Bon, the native religion already rooted in the high mountains.

Neither faith simply won. Tucci shows them mixing over centuries, borrowing gods, rites, and ideas until a distinct Tibetan Buddhism emerged from both. His learning rests on Tibetan texts, temple art, and years of travel in the region itself. The book is a landmark of Asian studies, and the full text gives readers his account whole, from the first diffusion of Buddhism onward.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cybervault_Cyber_: Israel built one of the world's most admired cybersecurity establishments, pairing military units that train teenage hackers with a startup sector that sells their skills worldwide. A National Security Archive cyber brief, published on May 22, 2018, surveys that establishment and its record. The brief sits in the Archive's Cyber Vault, which collects the public and declassified record of how states organize for conflict in cyberspace. For readers comparing national models, Israel is the standard case of a small country turning compulsory service and technical education into strategic weight online.
nasa-tm-19650010163-the-role-of-research:
John L Sloop, NASA's assistant associate administrator for advanced research and technology, gave this lecture on October 22, 1964. He spoke to Santa Clara County science teachers at Ames Research Center. His subject was the part research plays in crewed space flight.

Sloop frames the Moon landing plan as one step in a longer process. He says reaching that goal would boost science and technology, and national prestige and security. He also links space work to daily life. The lecture shows how NASA explained its research program to teachers in 1964. For teachers, that link between classroom science and national goals was the practical point of the talk.
nasa-tm-19680010567-a-mission-tracking-c:
Goddard Space Flight Center's Tracking and Data Systems Directorate produced this study in September 1967. It is the directorate's contribution to Phase A of the Galactic Jupiter Probe study at Goddard. Phase A was the early planning phase for the proposed deep space mission. The report presents a mission analysis together with the tracking, communication, and flight operation studies that support it.

A study cadre from the directorate carried out the work under cadre leader Richard Lehnert. Chapters were chaired separately for mission analysis, ground network support, communication and data handling, and flight operations. The catalog record names the supporting topics. They include ground network help, trajectory and guidance work, and flight operations. All support a spacecraft billions of kilometers away. Together the chapters ask what it would take, from the ground, to fly a probe to Jupiter.
nasa-tm-19700015586-relative-motion-of-t:
E. R. Lancaster of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in April 1970. It treats the relative motion of two particles, each moving in its own elliptic orbit under gravity. Work of this kind helps predict how two orbiting bodies drift toward or away from each other over time.

Lancaster notes that papers over the past decade offered only approximate solutions to this problem. Those solutions assumed the gap and speed difference between the particles stay small beside their own positions and speeds. His paper works through the problem with a full set of defined symbols and orbit terms. A worked numerical example near the end shows the method in use.
nasa-tm-19700030131-glossary-of-terms-pe:
The Kennedy Space Center issued this glossary in June 1970. It defines the terms used in reliability and quality assurance work at the center. Staff across many offices needed one shared set of meanings for their checks and reviews.

Entries run from basic ideas, such as acceptable quality level, onward through the field. The acceptable quality level is given as a rate of defects that a batch may show. The book was kept current by the center's Quality Assurance Directorate. Changes and supplements were issued as the need arose. A shared vocabulary keeps inspection fair and reports clear.
nasa-tm-19720004489-redundancy-managemen:
Richard A Campbell of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on November 9, 1971, as NASA TM X-64625. He worked in the Astrionics Laboratory. The subject is backup management for electrohydraulic servoactuators. These powered units move control surfaces and engine parts. If one fails in flight, a spare must take over cleanly. Campbell's system watches for that moment using mathematics, not extra sensors.

A mathematical model of a healthy actuator runs beside the real ones. A compensation network adjusts the model for outside disturbances. When a real unit drifts from the model, the system can flag the fault. It can then switch control to a sound spare. The report presents the full model reference design.
podcast-dannyjones-CwcIqRaSbLI:
Anjan Katta works on technology designed to cut the health costs of screens. He brings Danny Jones a warning attributed to Steve Jobs. In that warning, blue light from devices is making people sick. Katta argues Jobs limited his own children's screen time because he understood what the light does to eyes, sleep, and brains.

The episode covers the biology as Katta presents it: circadian rhythms broken by evening light, eye strain, and the deeper effects he links to modern disease. Jones tests the claims against his own habits, as listeners will. Some of the science here, light and sleep, is well established; the larger claims are Katta's. The conversation works as a practical brief for changing how a household uses screens, whatever a listener decides about its strongest assertions.
podcast-dannyjones-WMnIyiFnlLI:
Randall Carlson tells Danny Jones why humans need to leave Earth soon, in an entry from the Danny Jones podcast. Carlson, the catastrophist who studies cosmic impacts, argues that our planet's calm is a lucky break that will end. Jones hosts him in a long, curious interview format.

Carlson lays out the record of past strikes and what one large impact would do to cities, farms, and climate. He argues that spreading to other worlds is not adventure but insurance. The talk gives his warning its starkest form, and it suits listeners who met him on Rogan's show and want the pure case.
podcast-dannyjones-WmD3uDMH7LI:
Dr. Rick Strassman, the best known researcher of the drug DMT, joins Danny Jones for a long talk. The episode title ties his secret research to biblical prophecy and the CIA. Strassman ran early legal studies in which volunteers took DMT under watch.

Strassman tells what his volunteers reported, including beings they said they met while on the drug. The talk moves from lab results to scripture and to claims about agency interest in his work. Listeners hear a rare mix of hard lab work and open wonder. The library keeps the episode as an archive record, without judging the claims.
podcast-tuckercarlson-LaH2QalhJLI:
Bret Weinstein is the evolutionary biologist who left academia in a famous campus fight. He sits with Tucker Carlson to debate the largest questions either man hosts. They include evolution itself, the existence of God, and Israel. They also include whether artificial intelligence will gain consciousness. The conversation is billed as a debate, and both men arrive with positions.

Weinstein argues from biology toward a cautious openness on faith; Carlson argues from conviction toward the gaps in materialism. Their exchange on Israel places an ally of the country beside one of its sharpest critics on the right. Nothing is settled, which is the format's honesty. The recording preserves two of independent media's biggest names testing each other's worldviews at length, a specimen of the long-form argument that replaced the television segment for their shared audience.
rico-and-wiseli:
Johanna Spyri's tales of Swiss children appear here in Louise Brooks's translation, in two stories bound together. The first, Rico and Stineli, runs to twenty-one chapters in the contents. The second, How Wiseli Was Provided For, follows it and gives the volume its joint title.

Rico's story moves from a quiet house and school days to the old schoolmaster's fiddle. A beautiful, distant lake without a name draws him, and a sad house gives the lake a name at last. Chapters on his mother, a precious legacy, and a long journey lead to the Lake of Sils and then to sunshine on the Lake of Garda. Two happy travellers cross the mountains home.
ten-years-exile-memoirs-of-that-interest: The Baroness de Stael-Holstein wrote Ten Years' Exile. She set the memoirs down in 1810, 1811, 1812, and 1813. Her son first printed them from her own manuscript. Treuttel and Wurtz of London issued the book in 1821. The text was rendered from the French. Chapter heads name the causes of Bonaparte's enmity. They name strife in the Tribunate and Fouche. They name the Marengo campaign and the Infernal Machine. The Peace of Luneville, Paris in 1801, and a trip to Coppet follow.
the-latin-irish-lives-of-ciaran-translat:
R. A. Stewart-Macalister edited early lives of Saint Ciaran for a Christian literature series, issued in London and New York in 1921. The contents promise a harmony of four lives, three Latin lives, an Irish life, notes, and a Latin text. His scholarly pages discuss manuscripts held in the Bodleian Library.

Two manuscripts, Rawlinson B 485 and B 505, carry the second Latin life, and one copies the other directly. Scholars disagree on their dates by more than a century. Readers interested in Celtic saints get both translated lives and the source problems behind them, set out in plain academic detail.
the-new-machiavelli:
H. G. Wells's novel The New Machiavelli is present here only through its contents and the heading of its first chapter, so the narrative does not appear. The contents divide the novel into four books. Book the First, The Making of a Man, covers a book that was never written, Bromstead and the narrator's father, schooldays, and adolescence.

Book the Second, Margaret, follows its heroine from Staffordshire to London and Venice and a house in Westminster. Book the Third, The Heart of Politics, takes up the riddle for the statesman, secession, and the besetting of sex. Book the Fourth, Isabel, closes with Love and Success, The Impossible Position, and The Breaking Point.
the-outdoor-girls-at-wild-rose-lodge-or-:
Laura Lee Hope published The Outdoor Girls at Wild Rose Lodge in 1921, subtitled The Hermit of Moonlight Falls. The contents list twenty-five chapters. Chapter One, Just Fun, opens on a wonderful day. The four Outdoor Girls rush over a dusty country road at thirty miles an hour in Mollie Billette's touring car. Mollie drives, Grace Ford sits beside her, and Betty Nelson and Amy ride behind.

Later chapter titles promise a falling tree, a queer little man, and a hold-up. A whirlpool, a moonlight apparition, and a tragedy follow. The hermit of the subtitle waits at Moonlight Falls. Hope gives her girls speed, scenery, and a mystery in the woods.
the-renaissance-of-the-vocal-art-a-pract:
Edmund J. Myer presents a practical study of singing dated 1902, arguing that vitality and vitalized energy, aroused through flexible and elastic bodily movements, engage the physical, mental, and emotional powers of the singer. His preface thanks friends, pupils, critics, and the profession for kind notices of earlier books.

Myer hopes the new volume will clarify principles set out in his work on position and action in singing for readers who missed them there. A motto warns against ridiculing anything new in art too quickly. Singers and teachers meet a movement-based voice method stated with missionary confidence.
the-seigneurs-of-old-canada-a-chronicle-:
William Bennett Munro wrote The Seigneurs of Old Canada, subtitled A Chronicle of New-World Feudalism. It is volume five of the Chronicles of Canada, a series in thirty-two volumes edited by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton. The imprint is Toronto, 1915. Chapter one is called An Outpost of Empire.

Munro opens with France rather than Canada. History without the Gallic race's picturesque annals is his opening question. From Charlemagne to the last Bonapartes, France counted in every reckoning, he says. She rallied neighbours in friendship at times, and made herself hated at others. France first brought orderly nationalism out of feudal chaos, he argues. Her Capet kings led crusades to Palestine. Yet the France of Austerlitz became the France of Waterloo within years, he notes.
the-shame-of-motley-being-the-memoir-of-: Rafael Sabatini's The Shame of Motley is dated 1908 in its header. The book presents the memoir of Lazzaro Biancomonte, sometime fool of the court of Pesaro. The pages shown here give the title and the start of the contents only. A sibling record of this same book carries the opening of chapter one. Part one, Flower of the Quince, ends with the fall of Pesaro. Part two, The Ogre of Cesena, begins with Madonna's summons. The list shown stops at chapter fourteen, Requiescat. No narrative text appears in this record.
the-standard-household-effect-company-fr:
William Dean Howells offers this humorous essay from his Literature and Life series, built around a friend's complaint about modern housekeeping. The friend arrives before the narrator has left town. He sighs at the furniture in its summer shrouds. He then describes his own house after a month of the eternal-womanly. The rugs are up and the floors bare. Everything is tied, sewed, or moth-balled away.

Chandeliers wear draw-string bags, pictures hide in cheese-cloth, and mirrors are veiled in gauze so the man cannot see his own miserable face. He warns that granddaughters keep house far harder than grandmothers did. Their zeal, unchecked, will put an end to the eternal-womanly itself. He has been studying out a remedy. He calls it the standard household-effect company.
the-story-of-the-herschels-a-family-of-a:
A prefatory note dated 1886 introduces this family biography. It tells of three astronomers: Sir William Herschel, Sir John Herschel, and Caroline Herschel. The compiler gathered it from the best available sources. No compiler's name is printed on the pages present here. The note hopes the particulars will teach young readers two things. Knowledge brings real pleasure. Quietly doing one's duty brings solid happiness.

Biography's value needs no arguing, the writer insists. We learn to live good and honest lives by following good examples. Those who went before us set them. Young readers should take the Herschels' lessons to heart. A contents list follows, its first chapter praising astronomical study as a source of intellectual pleasure that leads the mind to wonder and adore.
the-tattva-muktavali:
Pûrnânanda Chakravartin, a native of Bengal, wrote the Tattva-muktâvalî, a Sanskrit poem printed in the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society in 1883. Professor E. B. Cowell edited and translated it, adding the introduction shown here. Cowell admits nothing is known of the poet's date and doubts the poem is the one named in older accounts. He places it later than the fourteenth century.

Cowell explains the poem's chief interest: it vigorously attacks the Vedânta system from the Pûrnaprajña school founded by Madhva in thirteenth-century South India. That school holds individual souls distinct from God, against Vedânta teaching. Students of Indian philosophy get a rare polemical poem with a careful scholarly guide to its doctrines and alliances.
three-times-and-out-told-by-private-simm: Private Simmons told his war story to Nellie L. McClung, who wrote Three Times and Out, published at Toronto, Boston, and New York in 1918. McClung dedicated it to Tom Bromley, a loyal comrade who failed through no lack of courage. Seven chapters are listed. Headings trace the route from how it started, through Belgium and into Germany, then a hospital, a prison camp, Rossbach, and the escape. The front pages and chapter list are what is on these pages, so Simmons's account itself does not appear.
verse-and-prose-for-beginners-in-reading:
Verse and Prose for Beginners in Reading, dated 1893, gathers pieces from English and American writing for young pupils. Its preface owns a secret at once: though the title joins verse and prose, verse fills nine tenths of the book. The prose is some two hundred proverbs and familiar sayings, some of them in rhyme, set in groups among the poems.

The preface ties the book to the Riverside Primer and Reader, which was meant to serve as a pupil's sole reading text. That primer had to give most of its room to practice work, with only a taste of real literature. This companion volume reverses the balance, offering more of the real thing: nursery rhymes, folk tales, and work by great masters of verse. Teachers get a bridge from school exercises to the wider world of English letters.
